newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS - Spain CPI moderates but rates seen on hold.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Spain CPI moderates but rates seen on hold.

text.p: Spanish inflation moderated to 1.5 percent in May, but economists said the Bank of Spain would wait until single currency worries eased before sanctioning another reduction in its key money market interest rate.
Spain reported on Friday that inflation was 1.5 percent year-on-year in May after 1.7 percent in April, achieving some of the most modest levels in nearly three decades.
"1.5 percent is an extremely good number. It highlights the market's extremely good fundamentals," said David Brown, chief European economist at Bear Stearns.

The rate has moderated sharply this year from 3.2 percent in December and for the first time in recent times fell below that of inflation hardliner Germany, whose May rate was 1.6 percent. It is the lowest rate since 1.3 percent in March 1969.
"Spanish inflation has been absolutely remarkable at least in terms of what was expected a year ago," said Donald Smith, European economist at HSBC.

In its twice yearly report, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development on Thursday underscored the strength of Spanish economic fundamentals and encouraged further Spanish interest rate declines.
The Bank of Spain has cut rates four times this year, making it twelve times in just 17 months. Its last move on May 16 brought the rate down to 5.25 percent from 5.50 percent.
"Monetary policy remains tight...A further cautious relaxation of monetary policy may be expected following the consolidation of recent inflation gains," the OECD said.
But despite benign inflation and the OECD's urging, economists expect the Bank of Spain to hold steady at its next opportunity, the regular repo auction on Monday.

"We think they'll end the year close to four percent largely as confidence grows in the European Economic and Monetary Union and Spain's part in the first wave but I don't foresee a rate cut short term," Smith said.

The Bank of Spain wants to ensure the European summit in Amsterdam on June 16 and 17 approves a stability pact designed to ensure fiscal discipline after the launch of the euro in 1999, calming worries about progress on the single currency.

"In my opinion, it is most likely that it (the Bank of Spain) does not cut rates at its auction on Monday. It would prefer to wait for all the unknowns to be cleared up at the Amsterdam summit," said Juan Elias, economist at Caixa de Pensiones in Barcelona.
Although many economists do not expect the central bank to lower its rate on Monday, many do see a reduction at the following auction on June 24 once euro doubts are resolved.
In a Reuter survey of 13 economists conducted after the data, 12 said the Bank of Spain would keep rates steady on Monday, but seven foresaw a cut on June 24.

"With this number the Bank of Spain has scope to lower rates. Nonetheless, it would be more sensible to wait for the result of the Amsterdam summit so there are no unwelcome suprises," said Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist at Bank of America in Madrid.
